findings: 130 faculty have an h-index above 10 on papers with fewer than 100 authors (132 on all papers); 262 papers are in journals with impact factor above 10 and have fewer than 100 authors.

The Q1 share moved from 74% (2016–18) to 62% (2023–25) with year-matched quartiles, and from 75% to 70% with each journal's 2017 quartile frozen; on the fixed JCR yardstick the share in IF > 5 journals went from 19% to 23%.
Citing an institution and co-authoring with it go together only loosely (Spearman 0.55 between external citations and joint papers across 2495 Indian institutions).
The Indian partner backbone keeps 270 of 4742 institution links (42% of joint-paper weight) at α = 0.05.

A journal's impact factor says little about one paper: the median within-year Spearman correlation between IF and a paper's citations is 0.41; 28% of non-Q1 papers beat the median Q1 paper on normalised citations.
Of the classic bibliometric laws, these hold in our data: Lotka (1926), Bradford (1934), Seglen (1997), Pareto 80/20; see the table for the observed values.
Papers with an Indian hospital or medical partner get -16% citations (95% CI -25% to -5%) after year, field, lab and team size; foreign partners +23%.

Year-on-year changes in a faculty member's output follow a Laplace distribution better than a normal one (AIC 10,129 vs 10,740; 245 faculty), as Zhang et al. found for computer scientists. Their lag-1 autocorrelation is -0.39 (95% CI -0.44 to -0.35): between a pure random walk (0) and noise around a fixed personal level (-0.50), so each person's level drifts slowly.

A truncated random walk with those steps reproduces the share of zero-output years (24% vs 24% observed) and the inequality of total output (Gini 0.46 vs 0.43): luck alone produces most of the spread between faculty.
Rank persists (Matthew effect): 62% of the top 10% by 2016–20 output are again in the top 10% in 2021–25, against 11% by chance (p = 0.000); Spearman 0.50.

methods.h_filtered: h-index recomputed on the faculty member's papers with fewer than 100 authors (all years).
methods.regrading: Each paper's journal quartile frozen at its 2017 Scimago value vs the year-matched quartile; JCR 2024 IF used as one fixed yardstick.
methods.citers: External citations (citing institution not one of our labs) vs joint papers per Indian institution; rising = citing papers in 2025 minus 2022.
methods.completeness: Share of papers (or roster faculty) with each field present in OpenAlex or the roster.
methods.precision: Seeded random sample of 50 paper–faculty links, stratified by how the affiliation was matched; checked by hand by the team.
methods.local_global: Indian share = citations from Indian institutions outside our labs ÷ all citations; papers with ≥ 20 citations.
methods.mechanisms: For each Indian institution with ≥ 30 citations: citing papers, our papers cited per citing paper, the share from citing papers that cite ≥ 5 of ours (stacking), and the most common citing journal.
methods.backbone: Disparity filter (Serrano, Boguñá & Vespignani 2009, α = 0.05) on Indian institution co-authorship from our papers with ≤ 50 authors.
methods.payoff: OLS of log(1 + citations) on partner-type indicators with lab, year and field fixed effects, then adding log2 authors and review; HC1 errors; papers to 2025.
methods.q1: OLS of log(1 + citations) on Q1 (or log2 IF) with controls; within-year Spearman of IF vs citations.
methods.laws: Lotka exponent by discrete maximum likelihood; Price's square-root rule; Bradford zones of equal papers; citation shares of the top papers.
methods.fragility: Headline recomputed after removing the named paper(s) or year.
methods.walk: Faculty-by-year paper counts (papers < 100 authors, 2016-2025, faculty with >= 3 papers); Laplace vs normal fit of yearly changes (AIC, KS); lag-1 autocorrelation with a faculty-block bootstrap and a within-person year-shuffle null; 200 truncated random walks per person (Zhang et al. 2026, course paper P1); top-decile persistence vs 2,000 permutations.
methods.jumps: Year-on-year changes above 25% (papers) or 50% (citations), with automatic drivers.
